summary: Comments on the proposed Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123 and RFC 127. Bob Long at SDC noticed that the order messages leave depends on the local Network Control Program, so commands might go out before data. The user's NCP should keep the early requests until the data arrives.

plainLanguage.summary: This note warns that computers may send network messages in a different order than a protocol expects. It also argues that a higher-level protocol should not dictate lower-level transmission details.

subtitle: Comments on message ordering and protocol boundaries in a proposed Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: The proposed Initial Connection Protocol could depend on message order and byte-size assumptions that individual NCP implementations did not share.
tldr.mechanism: Ari Shoshani describes a case where INIT commands could precede data and argues that the ICP should not override procedures of the Host-Host Protocol.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records design concerns and recommends considering them before the protocol is settled. It updates RFC 127.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 151 as Unknown and records that it updates RFC 127. It is a historical comment on early connection-protocol design.

sections.title: A Possible Message-Ordering Problem
sections.content:
Bob Long at SDC noticed that the order in which messages leave a host depends on its local Network Control Program. In SDC's implementation, commands can receive priority over data.

As a result, the server's final INIT commands in the sequence described by RFC 123 might leave before the data marked S on socket L. The RFC says the user's NCP should be ready to hold those INITs until the data arrives and the user process replies.
sections.plainLanguage: A host may send a command before the data that another host expects first. The receiver may need to hold that command until the data arrives.

sections.title: Keeping Protocol Levels Separate
sections.content:
Shoshani says the ICP is a third-level protocol and should not alter or ignore procedures of the second-level Host-Host Protocol. One example is byte size: RFC 123 suggests 32 bits for a connection, while the Host-Host rules leave the choice to the sender and say NCPs should accept sizes from 1 through 255 bits.

He also questions removing the ALL requirement and specifying that 32 bits be sent in one message, because he sees those as decisions for the lower protocol level.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection protocol should use the lower-level rules instead of changing them. Different hosts need room to choose the byte sizes their systems can handle.

sections.title: Implementation Consequences
sections.content:
The note points out that some hosts, including TIPs, may not be prepared to handle a fixed byte size or a particular message size. It argues that a higher-level protocol should avoid creating special cases that NCP implementations cannot support.

Shoshani presents these comments so network participants can consider them before the Atlantic City meeting.
sections.plainLanguage: Small or specialized hosts may have limits that larger hosts do not. The proposal should account for those differences before it is finalized.
